gloss: An official document that sets out the rights and rules of an organization or city.
examples: The city *charter* limits the mayor to two terms.
The school operates under a *charter* from the state.
Two *charters* were revoked after the audit.

gloss: A deep opening in the ground, or a wide gap between people or ideas.
examples: A deep *chasm* runs along the north side of the canyon.
There is a widening *chasm* between the two parties.
The hikers stopped at the edge of the *chasm*.

gloss: The state of not having sex, especially for religious or moral reasons.
examples: The monks take vows of poverty and *chastity*.
Her novel treats *chastity* as an old-fashioned virtue.
*Chastity* was expected of unmarried women at the time.

gloss: Quick, casual talk about unimportant things.
examples: The *chatter* in the hallway stopped when the teacher walked in.
I could hear the *chatter* of kids in the next room.
There is a lot of *chatter* online about the new phone.

gloss: An unreasonable belief that your own group or sex is better than others.
examples: The film was criticized for its casual *chauvinism*.
Male *chauvinism* was common in offices back then.
He mistook his *chauvinism* for patriotism.
contrast: The 'ch' is pronounced /ʃ/, like the 'sh' in *show*.

gloss: A person who believes their own group or sex is superior to others.
examples: Her boss was an old-fashioned *chauvinist*.
The comment made him sound like a *chauvinist*.
A few *chauvinists* still object to women on the crew.

gloss: Someone who hates spending money.
examples: Do not be a *cheapskate* — leave a decent tip.
My uncle is such a *cheapskate* that he washes paper plates.
*Cheapskates* love this place because the portions are huge.

gloss: A person who breaks the rules to win or to get an advantage.
examples: Everyone at the table knew he was a *cheat*.
She called him a liar and a *cheat*.
The site bans *cheats* from online matches.

gloss: A small book of blank checks issued by a bank.
examples: I found an old *checkbook* in the desk drawer.
He pulled out his *checkbook* and wrote her a check.
Both *checkbooks* are still in the safe.

gloss: A written list of things to do or check off one by one.
examples: The pilot went through the preflight *checklist*.
I made a *checklist* for the move.
Their *checklists* cover everything from tires to brake pads.

gloss: A firm yellow or white cheese with a sharp taste.
examples: Grate some *cheddar* over the potatoes.
This *cheddar* has been aged for two years.
He likes sharp *cheddar* on his burgers.

gloss: A rich dessert made of soft cheese on a crumb crust.
examples: She brought a strawberry *cheesecake* to the party.
One slice of *cheesecake*, two forks, please.
The diner makes three kinds of *cheesecake*.

gloss: The treatment of cancer with powerful drugs.
examples: He starts *chemotherapy* on Monday.
*Chemotherapy* left her exhausted for days.
The tumor shrank after six rounds of *chemotherapy*.

gloss: The square board of 64 light and dark squares used to play chess.
examples: He set the pieces up on the *chessboard*.
A folding *chessboard* fits in your bag.
The cafe keeps two *chessboards* by the window.

gloss: A V-shaped stripe or pattern, often worn on a sleeve to show rank.
examples: The sergeant wore three *chevrons* on his sleeve.
The rug has a gray *chevron* pattern.
Yellow *chevrons* mark the sharp curve ahead.
contrast: The 'ch' is pronounced /ʃ/, like the 'sh' in *shell*.

gloss: A plant whose leaves are eaten in salad and whose roasted root is added to coffee.
examples: New Orleans coffee is usually cut with *chicory*.
She grows *chicory* along the fence.
The blend tastes bitter because of the *chicory*.

gloss: A very small dog with big ears and short legs.
examples: Her *chihuahua* barks at everything.
Two *chihuahuas* were asleep on the couch.
A *chihuahua* weighs only a few pounds.
contrast: Spelled with 'hua' twice but pronounced chih-WAH-wah.

gloss: A thick spicy stew of ground meat, hot peppers, and often beans.
examples: He made a big pot of *chili* for the game.
This *chili* is too hot for me.
We had *chili* and cornbread for dinner.
contrast: Americans write *chili*; the British write *chilli*. It sounds almost like *chilly*.

gloss: A hope or idea that looks real but can never happen.
examples: Lasting peace there may be a *chimera*.
Critics called the plan a *chimera*.
He chased one *chimera* after another.

gloss: A pair of casual cotton pants, usually spoken of in the plural.
examples: He wore khaki *chinos* and a blue shirt.
These *chinos* need to be hemmed.
The store has *chinos* in four colors.

gloss: A smoked, dried jalapeno pepper, or a sauce made from it.
examples: Add a *chipotle* to the sauce for a smoky flavor.
The wings come with *chipotle* mayo.
Two *chipotles* were enough to make the chili spicy.
contrast: Say chih-POHT-lay; the last two letters are often flipped by mistake.

gloss: Treatment of pain by adjusting the spine and joints with the hands.
examples: He studied *chiropractic* for four years.
Her plan does not cover *chiropractic*.
Some doctors are skeptical of *chiropractic*.

gloss: A practitioner who treats pain by adjusting the spine and joints.
examples: My *chiropractor* sees me twice a month.
A *chiropractor* adjusted his neck.
Several *chiropractors* share the office.

gloss: Light, friendly talk about unimportant things.
examples: After a little *chitchat*, we got down to business.
He hates small talk and *chitchat*.
There was the usual *chitchat* about the weather.

gloss: Polite, protective behavior, especially by men toward women.
examples: He held the door and joked that *chivalry* is not dead.
The poem celebrates medieval *chivalry*.
*Chivalry* meant something different in the twelfth century.
contrast: The 'ch' is pronounced /ʃ/, like the 'sh' in *shiver*.

gloss: A common sexually transmitted infection caused by bacteria.
examples: *Chlamydia* often has no symptoms at all.
She was treated for *chlamydia* with antibiotics.
The clinic offers free testing for *chlamydia*.

gloss: A sweet-smelling liquid whose fumes make a person lose consciousness.
examples: The villain used a rag soaked in *chloroform*.
*Chloroform* was once used as an anesthetic.
The lab keeps *chloroform* in a locked cabinet.

gloss: The green substance in plants that lets them make food from sunlight.
examples: *Chlorophyll* gives leaves their green color.
In the fall, trees stop producing *chlorophyll*.
The experiment measures *chlorophyll* in pond water.

gloss: The tiny part of a plant cell where photosynthesis takes place.
examples: Photosynthesis happens inside the *chloroplasts*.
Draw a *chloroplast* and label its parts.
Animal cells have no *chloroplasts*.

gloss: A grip around someone's neck that stops them breathing, or tight control over something.
examples: The city banned the use of *chokeholds* by police.
He put the man in a *chokehold*.
A few companies have a *chokehold* on the market.

gloss: A narrow place where traffic, goods, or people can easily be blocked.
examples: The strait is a *choke point* for global oil shipments.
That bridge is the worst *choke point* on my commute.
Engineers looked for *choke points* in the supply chain.

gloss: A short necklace worn tight around the neck.
examples: She wore a black velvet *choker*.
*Chokers* came back in style a few years ago.
The *choker* sat tight against her neck.

gloss: A serious disease of the intestines spread by dirty water.
examples: An outbreak of *cholera* followed the flood.
*Cholera* spreads through contaminated water.
Aid workers vaccinated the camp against *cholera*.

gloss: A fatty substance in the blood that can block the arteries when there is too much of it.
examples: My doctor says my *cholesterol* is too high.
Eggs used to be blamed for raising *cholesterol*.
The pill lowered his *cholesterol* in three months.

gloss: A helicopter (informal).
examples: A news *chopper* circled over the freeway.
They flew the injured hiker out by *chopper*.
Two *choppers* landed in the field.

gloss: A thick soup usually made with fish or clams, potatoes, and milk.
examples: We ordered clam *chowder* and a sandwich.
The *chowder* comes in a bread bowl.
Her corn *chowder* is famous around here.

gloss: A thread of DNA in a cell that carries the genes.
examples: Humans have 46 *chromosomes*.
The test looks for damage to a single *chromosome*.
*Chromosomes* carry our genes.

gloss: Someone who is easily fooled (informal).
examples: I felt like a *chump* for believing him.
Do not let them treat you like a *chump*.
The scam took thousands of *chumps* for a few hundred dollars each.

gloss: A thick, solid piece of something, or a large part of a whole.
examples: Cut the beef into large *chunks*.
A *chunk* of ice fell off the roof.
Rent eats up a big *chunk* of my paycheck.

gloss: A person who attends church regularly.
examples: Most of his neighbors are regular *churchgoers*.
She is not a *churchgoer*, but she likes the music.
*Churchgoers* filled the parking lot on Sunday.

gloss: The rate at which customers or employees leave and are replaced.
examples: The company is fighting high customer *churn*.
*Churn* among nurses has doubled since 2020.
They track *churn* every quarter.

gloss: A steep tube or slide that things drop down.
examples: Toss the sheets down the laundry *chute*.
The mail *chute* is next to the elevator.
Both trash *chutes* were blocked.

gloss: A thick, spicy sauce of fruit or vegetables served with food.
examples: The curry came with mango *chutney*.
Spread a little *chutney* on the sandwich.
She makes her own tomato *chutney*.

gloss: Bold nerve, in a way that is either shocking or admirable.
examples: It took real *chutzpah* to ask for a raise on his first day.
I have to admire her *chutzpah*.
He had the *chutzpah* to argue with the judge.
contrast: The initial 'ch' is pronounced like an 'h': HUUT-spuh.

gloss: A tight roll of tobacco leaves for smoking.
examples: He lit a *cigar* on the porch.
The room smelled of *cigars*.
She handed out *cigars* when the baby was born.

gloss: A thin paper tube of tobacco for smoking.
examples: He smokes a pack of *cigarettes* a day.
She stepped outside for a *cigarette*.
*Cigarettes* cost almost ten dollars a pack here.

gloss: Something very easy to do (informal).
examples: The test was a *cinch*.
Installing the app is a *cinch*.
Finding parking downtown is no *cinch*.

gloss: A small piece of burned coal or wood that is no longer flaming.
examples: *Cinders* from the fire pit were still warm.
A *cinder* burned a hole in his jacket.
The path was covered with *cinders* for traction.

gloss: A system for writing a message in code.
examples: The letters were written in a simple *cipher*.
Codebreakers cracked the *cipher* in a week.
Modern *ciphers* are almost impossible to break by hand.

gloss: The system of electrical circuits inside a device.
examples: Water damaged the *circuitry* in the laptop.
The *circuitry* of a modern car is incredibly complex.
She studies the *circuitry* of the brain.

gloss: An operation that removes the fold of skin at the end of the penis.
examples: The hospital performs *circumcision* on request.
*Circumcision* is part of the religious ceremony.
The clinic does about twenty *circumcisions* a month.

gloss: A fact or condition that affects a situation.
examples: Under the *circumstances*, they did their best.
He died in strange *circumstances*.
I cannot imagine any *circumstance* where that would be legal.

gloss: Thin, wispy cloud that forms very high in the sky.
examples: Thin *cirrus* streaked the sky all afternoon.
*Cirrus* usually means a change in the weather is coming.
By noon the *cirrus* had thickened into a gray layer.

gloss: Fruit such as oranges, lemons, and limes, or the trees that bear them.
examples: Florida is famous for its *citrus*.
One hard frost can ruin the whole *citrus* crop.
He cannot eat *citrus* because of his stomach.

gloss: A view or picture of a city.
examples: The photo shows the *cityscape* at dusk.
New towers have changed the *cityscape*.
She paints *cityscapes* in oil.

gloss: Polite behavior toward other people, especially in public life.
examples: The debate was short on *civility*.
He treated even his critics with *civility*.
There is a real hunger for *civility* in politics.

gloss: A person who asks for money or a right they believe is theirs.
examples: The *claimant* filed for unemployment benefits.
Each *claimant* must provide proof of income.
Lawyers here represent about forty *claimants*.

gloss: Loud noise from many voices, or a loud public demand.
examples: The *clamor* of the crowd drowned him out.
Public *clamor* finally forced the mayor to act.
After the report came out, the *clamor* for his resignation grew.

gloss: A sudden, strict effort by authorities to stop something.
examples: The city announced a *clampdown* on illegal parking.
There has been a *clampdown* on overtime spending.
Border *clampdowns* slowed shipments for weeks.

gloss: A loud ringing sound made by metal hitting metal.
examples: The gate shut with a *clang*.
We heard the *clang* of a hammer on steel.
Each *clang* of the bell echoed down the street.

gloss: The quality of being easy to see, hear, or understand.
examples: The contract lacks *clarity* on who pays for repairs.
I need some *clarity* before I decide.
The lake is known for the *clarity* of its water.

gloss: A short fight or sharp disagreement between people or groups.
examples: There were violent *clashes* between police and protesters.
The two men had a *clash* over money.
A scheduling *clash* forced us to cancel.

gloss: A book, film, or object of lasting high quality.
examples: That movie is a *classic*.
The novel became an American *classic*.
He collects *classics* from the 1960s.

gloss: Schoolwork done during class rather than at home.
examples: Half the grade comes from *classwork*.
He missed a week of *classwork* while he was sick.
Finish your *classwork* before you start the homework.

gloss: The loud noise of hard objects knocking together.
examples: The *clatter* of dishes came from the kitchen.
I heard the *clatter* of hooves on the pavement.
The room went quiet except for the *clatter* of keyboards.

gloss: The collarbone, joining the breastbone to the shoulder.
examples: He broke his *clavicle* in the crash.
The X-ray showed a crack in the left *clavicle*.
Both *clavicles* healed without surgery.

gloss: The work of making a place or thing clean.
examples: Spring *cleaning* took us the whole weekend.
Who does the *cleaning* in your house?
The rug needs a deep *cleaning*.

gloss: A heavy knife with a wide blade, used for chopping meat and bone.
examples: The butcher split the ribs with a *cleaver*.
Hang the *cleaver* on the magnetic strip.
Two *cleavers* were missing from the kitchen.

gloss: Mercy shown by an official, especially by reducing a punishment.
examples: The governor granted *clemency* to three prisoners.
His family is asking for *clemency*.
The board denied her petition for *clemency*.

gloss: A man who is an official leader in a Christian church.
examples: A local *clergyman* spoke at the funeral.
Several *clergymen* signed the letter.
The *clergyman* met the family at the door.

gloss: A religious leader in any faith.
examples: A senior *cleric* condemned the attack.
*Clerics* from three faiths attended.
The *cleric* led the prayer.

gloss: An ending that leaves you in suspense, or a contest whose result stays in doubt.
examples: The season ended on a *cliffhanger*.
The election turned into a *cliffhanger*.
The show is famous for its *cliffhangers*.

gloss: The most exciting or important point of a story or event.
examples: The chase scene is the *climax* of the film.
Tension built to a *climax* in the third act.
The trial reached its *climax* with her testimony.

gloss: An act of going up something steep.
examples: It is a steep *climb* to the summit.
The last *climb* took us two hours.
They made three *climbs* in one weekend.

gloss: The fact or event that finally settles something.
examples: The free parking was the *clincher* for me.
His confession was the *clincher* for the jury.
For a lot of buyers, the warranty is the *clincher*.

gloss: A doctor or nurse who treats patients directly rather than doing only research.
examples: The study surveyed 200 *clinicians*.
She is a researcher as well as a *clinician*.
*Clinicians* say the new guidelines are hard to follow.

gloss: A piece cut out of a newspaper, or a piece cut off something.
examples: She kept newspaper *clippings* about the trial.
Rake the grass *clippings* off the lawn.
He mailed me a *clipping* from the local paper.

gloss: A mechanism of gears and springs that is wound up to make something move.
examples: The old toy runs on *clockwork*.
Everything went like *clockwork*.
The museum repairs antique *clockwork*.

gloss: A living thing grown from the cells of another and genetically identical to it, or an exact copy of something.
examples: The sheep was a *clone* of an adult ewe.
The phone is a cheap *clone* of a famous brand.
Scientists produced several *clones*.

gloss: The process of making a genetically identical copy of a living thing.
examples: *Cloning* raises hard ethical questions.
Human *cloning* is banned in most countries.
The lab specializes in the *cloning* of plants.

gloss: A photograph or shot taken from very near the subject.
examples: The camera cut to a *close-up* of her face.
Take a *close-up* of the label so I can read it.
The film uses a lot of *close-ups*.
contrast: The 's' is /s/, as in *close* (near), not the /z/ of the verb *to close*.

gloss: The final meeting at which the sale of a house or property is completed.
examples: *Closing* is set for the fifteenth.
We signed about thirty documents at the *closing*.
*Closing* costs came to four thousand dollars.

gloss: The shutting of a road, business, or facility, either for a time or for good.
examples: The storm caused road *closures* across the county.
The plant *closure* will cost 400 jobs.
Check the district website for school *closures*.

gloss: A thick lump that forms when blood becomes solid.
examples: A blood *clot* in his leg sent him to the hospital.
The medicine keeps *clots* from forming.
Doctors found a small *clot* near the lung.

gloss: Power or influence, especially in politics or business.
examples: The union still has real *clout* in this state.
She used her *clout* to get the meeting.
The paper has lost much of its *clout*.

gloss: The activity of going out to nightclubs.
examples: They went *clubbing* until three in the morning.
*Clubbing* is not really my thing.
He gave up *clubbing* after the baby was born.

gloss: A building used by the members of a club or a sports team.
examples: We will meet at the *clubhouse* after the round.
Reporters waited outside the *clubhouse*.
Both *clubhouses* were remodeled last year.

gloss: The work of training a team or advising a person.
examples: He went into *coaching* after he retired.
The team's *coaching* has improved a lot this year.
She offers career *coaching* over video calls.

gloss: A thin layer of something spread over a surface.
examples: The pan has a nonstick *coating*.
A thin *coating* of dust covered everything.
These *coatings* protect the metal from rust.

gloss: A stand or rail with hooks for hanging coats.
examples: Hang your jacket on the *coat rack*.
The *coat rack* by the door is full.
They bought two *coat racks* for the entryway.

gloss: A hard silver-gray metal used in batteries and in a deep blue dye.
examples: Most *cobalt* comes from just a few mines.
Batteries need *cobalt* and lithium.
The vase is a deep *cobalt* blue.

gloss: A number placed before a variable in an equation, or a number that measures a property.
examples: Multiply by the *coefficient* of friction.
In 3x, the *coefficient* is 3.
The two *coefficients* have to be equal.

gloss: The use of force or threats to make someone do something.
examples: She signed the confession under *coercion*.
The court found no evidence of *coercion*.
They rely on persuasion, not *coercion*.

gloss: The state of living or existing together without fighting.
examples: The treaty promised peaceful *coexistence*.
Ranchers say *coexistence* with wolves is possible.
Years of *coexistence* ended in violence.

gloss: A sweet cake with a crumbly topping, eaten with coffee.
examples: She baked a cinnamon *coffee cake* for the meeting.
There is *coffee cake* in the break room.
The bakery sells three kinds of *coffee cake*.

gloss: A tall pot used to brew or serve coffee.
examples: The *coffeepot* is empty again.
He filled the *coffeepot* with water.
Two *coffeepots* sat on the warmer.

gloss: A store of money belonging to a government or organization, usually used in the plural.
examples: The tax brought millions into the state's *coffers*.
City *coffers* are nearly empty.
The scandal drained the party's *coffers*.

gloss: One of two or more people who started a company or organization together.
examples: She is the *co-founder* of a software company.
Both *co-founders* left after the sale.
He met his *co-founder* in grad school.

gloss: A tooth on a wheel that turns another wheel, or a small unimportant part of a large organization.
examples: One broken *cog* stopped the whole machine.
He felt like a *cog* in a huge company.
The *cogs* on the old gear were worn smooth.

gloss: A word that shares an origin with a word in another language.
examples: English 'night' and German 'Nacht' are *cognates*.
Spanish learners can lean on *cognates*.
'Mother' has a *cognate* in almost every European language.

gloss: The mental process of thinking, learning, and understanding.
examples: The drug can affect memory and *cognition*.
Researchers study *cognition* in young children.
Losing sleep hurts *cognition*.

gloss: The quality of fitting together in a clear, logical way.
examples: The essay has good ideas but no *coherence*.
His story lacked *coherence*.
Voters are looking for *coherence* between promises and policy.

gloss: The state of a group sticking together as a unit.
examples: The team lost its *cohesion* after the trade.
Social *cohesion* takes years to build.
The party is struggling to keep its *cohesion*.

gloss: A group of people who share something, especially the same age or starting year.
examples: The study followed a *cohort* of 5,000 nurses.
This year's *cohort* of students is the largest yet.
Both *cohorts* showed the same pattern.

gloss: A newly invented word or phrase.
examples: 'Selfie' is a recent *coinage*.
The book is full of odd *coinages*.
That term is a *coinage* of the 1990s.

gloss: A surprising case of two things happening together by chance.
examples: It was pure *coincidence* that we sat next to each other.
I do not believe in *coincidences*.
By an odd *coincidence*, we share a birthday.

gloss: The share of a medical bill you pay yourself after the deductible is met.
examples: After the deductible, your *coinsurance* is twenty percent.
*Coinsurance* can add up fast on a hospital stay.
Check the plan's *coinsurance* before you choose it.

gloss: A cold salad of shredded cabbage in a creamy dressing.
examples: The barbecue comes with beans and *coleslaw*.
She makes *coleslaw* with vinegar instead of mayo.
There is a tub of *coleslaw* in the fridge.

gloss: A person you work with on a project.
examples: Her longtime *collaborator* wrote the music.
The two *collaborators* met in Chicago.
He thanked his *collaborators* in the preface.

gloss: Large dark green leaves cooked as a vegetable, common in Southern cooking.
examples: She cooked *collard greens* with ham hocks.
*Collard greens* need to simmer for an hour.
We had cornbread and *collard greens*.

gloss: An object people collect because it may become valuable.
examples: That lunchbox is now a *collectible*.
He sells vintage *collectibles* online.
Some *collectibles* gain value fast.

gloss: A group of people who own or run something together.
examples: The farm is run by a *collective*.
They formed an artists' *collective* downtown.
Several *collectives* share the warehouse.

gloss: A person who gathers objects of one kind as a hobby or investment.
examples: He is a serious *collector* of vintage guitars.
*Collectors* paid thousands for the poster.
The museum bought it from a private *collector*.
